long: MagenticLite is the next generation of Magentic-UI from Microsoft AI Frontiers. The project README describes it as an agentic application that pairs an on-device-friendly orchestrator model, MagenticBrain, with a browser-use model, Fara, so tasks can run without frontier-scale models.

It works across the browser and the local file system: web research, form filling, and file management in one workflow. The README says it stops and checks in before critical actions, and that browser sessions run inside a Quicksand VM sandbox so the agent cannot reach the rest of the machine unless you allow it.

The AgentScout listing still describes the project as an experimental human-in-the-loop agent. The limitations doc calls MagenticLite a research prototype. The earlier 0.1 release, aimed at frontier models, stays on the magentic-ui-0.1 branch.
magentic-ui.who: People who want a local agent for browser tasks and local files, with a check-in before critical actions, and researchers comparing small-model agent setups. The README's quick start is written for macOS and Windows (WSL). Other platforms are in the installation guide.
features: Orchestrator (MagenticBrain) plus a browser-use model (Fara), aimed at small models rather than frontier-scale compute
Browser and local file workflows in one app, including research, forms, and file management
Check-in before critical actions, so you can steer, approve, or take over
Browser sessions inside the Quicksand VM sandbox
Installable from PyPI as magentic_ui 0.2.x; the 0.1 line remains on its own branch
pros: The README says it is built for small models and does not require frontier-scale compute.
You stay in the loop: it checks in before critical actions, and browser sessions sit in the Quicksand sandbox.
The code is under the MIT License, and the 0.2 line installs from PyPI.
cons: The limitations doc calls it a research prototype. Summaries of long sources often miss content, and long multi-turn chats get worse.
Steering the browser agent mid-task may not stick: MagenticBrain can send Fara back to the original sub-task.
Very large files do not fit, browser file-upload controls are not supported, and images are not supported as task inputs.
You still bring a model endpoint. The quick start is macOS or Windows via WSL.
setup: On macOS or Windows (WSL), create a directory and a Python 3.12 virtual environment with uv, then install the PyPI package magentic_ui at version 0.2.0 or newer.
Run magentic-ui --port 8081 and open http://127.0.0.1:8081/.
Finish the in-app onboarding to connect a model endpoint. The repo's model hosting guide covers standing one up.
For a from-source run, use the build-from-source doc. The previous 0.1 release is the magentic-ui-0.1 branch, not the default install.
Read docs/limitations.md before you give it a long summary, a file upload, or an image.
faq: What does Magentic-UI not handle well?

The project's limitations doc lists weak long-form summaries, degrading multi-turn chats, steering that the orchestrator may ignore, very large files, browser upload controls, and image inputs. It calls MagenticLite a research prototype.
The README's quick start installs magentic_ui 0.2.x from PyPI. That is MagenticLite. The Magentic-UI 0.1 release, aimed at frontier models, is on the magentic-ui-0.1 branch.

pros: Implementation and review are separate sessions. The listing describes a six-point merge gate: reviewer verdict, acceptance criteria, green CI, a clean branch, and an exact commit SHA.
Self-hosting is free under AGPL-3.0 or the Sustainable Use License, with your own model keys, via Docker or Node.js 22+.
Orbi Cloud includes 3 merged deliveries with no card, then Solo and Pro on the pricing page we cite.
cons: Cloud Solo is $24 a month and Pro is $66 a month, both billed yearly ($290 and $790), for 1 and 5 repos.
Work starts from GitHub labels (ai-ready, and ai-release for a tagged release). No label, no run.
Self-hosting still needs your own model keys. The app does not include a model.
setup: Self-host with Docker or Node.js 22+ (SQLite and local git worktrees), or install the Orbi Cloud GitHub App.
Add the ai-ready label to an issue to start an isolated worktree, a pull request, and the separate review session.
Let the six-point gate finish before you expect a merge. Apply ai-release when you want a tagged GitHub Release.
Read the official pricing page linked from the listing before you pick Solo or Pro.

pros: The hosted MCP endpoint is https://neverapply.co/mcp, with OAuth 2.1 and PKCE, so the client config does not hold a personal API key.
Applying requires the mcp:apply scope, credits, and an explicit confirmation of the job title and company. Screening answers are not guessed.
The Free tier is $0: 10 lifetime auto-applies, a 5-matches-a-day preview, and 50 MCP reads a day per client.
cons: Those free caps are the whole free plan. Pro is $29 a month (150 apply credits) and Max is $49 a month (450).
The job index is the maker's figure (919,000+ roles on the listing). It is not a count we re-crawled.
An assistant can prepare a resume and a cart of roles, but it cannot submit a named application until you confirm that job.
setup: Add https://neverapply.co/mcp as a remote Streamable HTTP MCP server in Claude, Cursor, Codex, ChatGPT, VS Code, Gemini CLI, Kiro, or Grok.
Complete the browser OAuth sign-in and grant mcp:read, mcp:write, or mcp:apply.
Or install the MIT-licensed plugin and skills from the kasovy/neverapply-mcp repository.
Confirm the plan's apply credits on neverapply.co/pricing before you expect submissions.

pros: MIT licensed and self-hosted. The stack (React 19, Java 21, Spring Boot, PostgreSQL) starts with one Docker Compose command.
An agent only sees the cards you connect, and a media proposal waits for approval before it spends model credits.
You can import a ComfyUI API workflow JSON, map the inputs, and save it as a tool on the canvas.
cons: OpenAI-compatible APIs, ComfyUI, and RunningHub are billed by those providers. Agenvas does not include their usage.
You run the Docker stack yourself, including PostgreSQL.
The GitHub star count on the listing is small. Popularity is not the reason to pick it.
setup: Clone the repo and start it with Docker Compose, as the listing describes.
Connect an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, a ComfyUI workflow, or a RunningHub app.
Put text, image, video, or audio on cards and connect only the cards the agent should see.
Approve the proposal card before a generation job runs.

pros: The Apache 2.0 code is still readable and forkable after the shutdown.
The README points existing users to Cline, the project Roo Code was forked from, and to ZooCode, a community fork.
The old mode design (Code, Architect, Ask, Debug, and custom modes) is still visible in the archived tree if you are studying it.
cons: The extension shut down on May 15, 2026, and the repository is archived. There is no maintained release.
It is a poor install for a new setup. The listing says roocode.com redirects to Roomote.
Billing questions for the old product go to billing@roocode.com, not to a current in-app plan.
setup: Do not install Roo Code for new work.
Read the archived README on github.com/RooCodeInc/Roo-Code.
If you want the maintained line it was forked from, open the Cline listing. ZooCode is the community fork the README names.
If you still have an old subscription, use the billing address in the FAQ rather than the archived extension.

pros: The Apache 2.0 code remains on GitHub and the team encourages a fork.
The archived product is still a useful map of a visual builder: Agentflow, Chatflow, tool calling, RAG, human review, and traces.
You can read the repo without an account.
cons: End of life was August 31, 2026. The repo was archived on August 13, 2026, and npm packages and Docker images were marked deprecated.
The core team stopped taking part on Discord and GitHub at end of life, so issues will not be fixed upstream.
A new project should not pin those deprecated images.
setup: Treat github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise as an archive.
If you already run a deployment, plan a fork or a move. Do not pull a fresh deprecated image and assume it is supported.
For a builder that is still maintained, use the no-code builders category and check each listing's maturity line.

pros: The repo still documents AgentChat, Core, extensions for model clients and MCP, and AutoGen Studio.
Microsoft's README names Microsoft Agent Framework as the successor and points at a migration guide.
Python 3.10 or later is the stated requirement if you are only reading or migrating an existing project.
cons: The README says the project is archived and no longer maintained: no bug fixes, security fixes, new features, or support, and it advises against production use.
AutoGen Studio is part of that archived tree, not a current hosted product.
Starting a new production agent on AutoGen means ignoring the maintainer's own advice.
setup: For new work, start with Microsoft Agent Framework and the migration guide linked from the AutoGen README.
To study the old APIs, clone github.com/microsoft/autogen and stay on Python 3.10 or newer.
Do not ship AutoGen Studio as if Microsoft were still supporting it.

pros: The app is free. The Microsoft Store listing says Free. Claude Code, Codex, and other accounts are signed in separately.
One desktop holds the terminal session, a web window the agent can drive, and a Git window for diffs and pushes.
Scheduled AI employees leave logins and payments as a request for a person, and the iPhone and Android apps continue the same session.
cons: Model use bills the Claude, Codex, or other account you connect. Orke does not include that usage.
macOS is macOS 26 or later on Apple Silicon. Linux is a server build you open in a browser, x86_64.
Plain terminals work without an AI account, but the agent features do not.
setup: Install Windows x64 from the Microsoft Store, the Apple Silicon DMG from GitHub Releases, or the Linux server build.
Sign in to the agent CLI you already use. Usage counts toward that account.
Review diffs in the Git window before you push.
If you turn on an AI employee, leave login and payment steps for yourself and read the work log it writes.

pros: The desktop app and engine are free and GPL-3.0. Workflows are node graphs, so each model and step is visible.
The maker says it can run large open models on as little as 4 GB of VRAM and 8 GB of RAM via asynchronous weight streaming.
The same graph can run locally or on Comfy Cloud, and Comfy Agent can draft a workflow you then inspect.
cons: Comfy Cloud is paid: Standard $20 a month ($16 yearly), Creator $35, Pro $100, Team $700, with Enterprise on request.
Local runs still need a machine that can hold the models you choose. Low VRAM is a maker claim, not a guarantee for every model.
Partner Nodes for closed models such as Nano Banana are separate from the open engine.
setup: Install the desktop app or the open-source engine from the official site or the Comfy-Org/ComfyUI repo.
Load or build a node graph. Open models named on the listing include Wan, LTX, and Hunyuan.
If you use Comfy Agent, read the graph it builds before you run it.
For hosted GPUs, compare the Cloud tiers on the pricing page cited in the listing. Yearly billing is about 20% less on the tiers that show a yearly price.

pros: The Professional cloud plan is $0, and the open-source edition (MPL-2.0) can be self-hosted.
An official MCP server and an open API let agents read and edit design files.
Files use SVG, CSS, HTML, and JSON, with design tokens plus CSS Grid and Flex layouts.
cons: Unlimited is $7 per editor a month, capped at $175. Enterprise is $25 per member a month. Private Server is $50k a year.
Self-hosting means you run the servers. The $0 cloud plan is the path that does not.
An agent with the MCP server can edit files. Grant that only to the files you mean it to touch.
setup: Use the Professional cloud plan or self-host the open-source edition from github.com/penpot/penpot.
Connect the official MCP server only if you want an agent to read or edit files.
Keep design tokens as the source of truth before you export.
Check penpot.app pricing before you add paid editors. Non-profit, education, and open-source discounts are mentioned on the pricing notes in the listing.

pros: One product covers recurring WhatsApp messages, custom commands, moderation, RSS and API news, Channel posts, and an engagement dashboard.
The official MCP server is remote Streamable HTTP at https://mcp.9bot.com.br/mcp with OAuth, using the WhatsApp number on the account.
Basic Pro starts with a 7-day trial. The site is offered in English, Portuguese, Spanish, and Chinese.
cons: After the trial, Basic Pro is US$35 a month for the first 3 months, then US$70 a month. MCP access needs an active subscription.
It is a WhatsApp groups, communities, and Channels product. It is not a general chat agent.
An agent can schedule and moderate only inside the 9bot account you connect. It does not replace WhatsApp's own rules.
setup: Start the 7-day trial on 9bot.com.br and connect the WhatsApp account that owns the groups.
Turn on the moderation rules and any RSS, live-stream, or affiliate schedules you actually want.
To drive it from an assistant, add https://mcp.9bot.com.br/mcp and sign in with OAuth using that WhatsApp number.
Confirm the subscription is active before you expect MCP tools to run. The listing says an active plan is required.
